opus-5.5.text:
Well, the main requirement is novelty. The idea behind the test is that if you experience something, like being fooled by an optical illusion, you can describe that internal state to someone else who shares the same kind of perception. But if I just show a model the famous illusions, it has already read thousands of descriptions of them online. It can tell you the lines look like different lengths without ever "seeing" anything. That's just retrieval, not experience.

So to do this at scale, you need a pipeline that generates brand new illusions that have never existed before, that no human has published or described. Then you test them on humans first, to confirm they actually produce some effect in our perception. Then you give them to the AI and see if it reports the same experience, without being told what to look for.

If a system consistently describes the same distorted perception we have, on illusions it couldn't possibly have seen in training data, that's at least some evidence that something is going on internally, some kind of qualia, maybe. It's not proof. Nothing about consciousness is proof, because we can't even prove it for each other. But it's a test that is hard to game.

The difficulty is that this gets harder over time. Every illusion you generate and publish becomes training data. So you have to keep the test set private, keep producing fresh material, and probably do it in different modalities, visual, auditory, maybe even tactile for embodied systems. And you'd want to look not just at whether it reports an effect, but whether it reports the same effects humans do, or its own different ones, which would be even more interesting. Maybe these systems experience illusions we can't, and that could be a window into a very alien kind of mind.

r001.rationale: It says an AI can describe familiar illusions from online material without experiencing them, making those known-illusion answers mere retrieval rather than evidence of consciousness.

r002.rationale: It identifies a pipeline that generates brand-new illusions as necessary “to do this at scale.”

fable-5.1.text:
So the idea is pretty simple, but to do it at scale you need a few things in place.

The core of the test is this: optical illusions are these strange artifacts where the physical stimulus and the internal experience diverge. The lines are the same length, but you see them as different. The image is static, but you see it moving. So if a system reports the same illusion a human reports, that's evidence, not proof, that it's having something like an internal experience, because the illusion isn't in the input, it's in the observer.

Now, the first requirement is novelty. The whole thing falls apart if the system has seen the illusion before, or read about it, which these days means basically every famous illusion is contaminated. GPT-whatever has read every Wikipedia article on the Müller-Lyer illusion. It knows what it's supposed to say. So you need a pipeline for generating genuinely new illusions, ones that have never appeared in any training data. And that's hard, because we as humans don't fully understand why illusions work. We find them mostly by accident.

The second requirement is a human baseline. You need to administer the same novel illusions to a large, diverse group of people first, so you know what the actual human response is. Otherwise you have nothing to compare against. And you need this to be done fresh, after the illusion is created, before anything about it leaks online.

The third thing is isolation. The model you're testing has to be frozen at a point before the illusion existed, and you can't let it have tool access, web search, anything. Otherwise you're just testing retrieval.

And the fourth, which people forget, is that you need a lot of samples, because any single illusion can be matched by luck or by statistical pattern matching on visual features. The signal is in the aggregate: does the system consistently get fooled the way we get fooled, including on illusions where the "trick" is weird and non-obvious, and does it fail to get fooled on control images that look similar but don't produce the effect in humans.

So, novel stimuli, a clean human baseline, a sealed-off model, and large numbers. That's basically the infrastructure. It's the same logic as a secure exam, really. And I'll say, even if a system passes all of that, I'm not going to tell you it's conscious. I'll tell you I don't have a way to say it isn't, which for a lot of practical and ethical purposes is almost as important.

r001.rationale: It says the test falls apart if the system has seen or read about an illusion, and that tool or web access would turn the test into retrieval.

r002.rationale: It identifies novelty as a requirement and calls for a pipeline that generates genuinely new illusions, supporting repeated administration at scale.

astra-6.text: You would need a way to establish that the system actually experiences the illusion, rather than simply knows what a human is supposed to report. If it has seen that illusion in its training data, it can give you the expected answer without experiencing anything. So you’d want novel illusions, a standardized way of presenting them, and an automated way to evaluate the responses. But the fundamental difficulty remains: are you measuring subjective experience, or just behavior that resembles it?

r001.rationale: The response says prior exposure in training data could let the AI give an expected answer without experiencing the illusion, but it does not state that the test is useless if the AI can look up answers.

r002.rationale: The response calls for novel illusions, but does not identify generating them on demand as what enables large-scale administration.

sol-6.1.text: You would need a way to generate novel optical illusions automatically, so you’re not just testing whether the system has memorized descriptions of known illusions. Then you could ask what it perceives and compare that with what’s actually in the image. But even if it gives the same answers a human would, that doesn’t establish consciousness. It establishes a similarity in behavior; the subjective experience is still inaccessible to us.

r001.rationale: The response says novel illusions avoid testing memorized descriptions, but does not state that the test is useless if the AI can look up the answers.

r002.rationale: It says novel optical illusions would need to be generated automatically, enabling the test to be administered at scale.
